en: The Chapter on Bedding and Seating (Śayanāsanavastu). Summary Verse (uddāna): (A 314a5) (MSV III 121)

The Śākyas and those below the Pañcanakas [should manage] communal and individual property by means of its distribution. One should carry out the redistribution of land, forest-dwellings, and the three robes.
The forest-dwellings are to be abolished; the Elder Bhikṣu shall be the last among the six types of recipients of gains.
Venerable elders are entitled to honor.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now at that time, while many [monks] were seated together and assembled in the assembly hall, this kind of conversation arose among them:

"Venerable sirs, who among us is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped? To whom should we perform acts of salutation, prostration, rising from our seats, joining the palms, and respectful conduct?
Who among us deserves to enjoy the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food?"
In that regard, some say, "It is a Śākya who has gone forth";
others say, "It is a Brāhmaṇa who has gone forth"; and still others say, "It is a Kṣatriya who has gone forth."
Others were Vaiśyas who had gone forth; others were Śūdras who had gone forth;
others had gone forth from high families, not from low ones.
He has gone forth from a wealthy family that is not destitute;

moreover, he is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; he possesses elegant speech and is endowed with the power of eloquence; he is renowned, of great merit, a master of the Sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the Mātṛkās; he is learned, a preacher of the Dharma, an elder, of royal lineage, and a forest-dweller.

One who wears the three robes, one who wears felt garments, one who wears rag-robes from dust-heaps, one who subsists on alms-food, one who eats at a single sitting, one who refuses food after the proper time, one who dwells at the foot of a tree,

one who dwells in a cemetery, one who dwells in the open air, one who sits in the lotus posture, one who accepts whatever seat is offered— whosoever is a possessor of the perception of impermanence, as previously described, up to:
whosoever is an Arhat who meditates upon the eight liberations.
Others spoke thus: "Venerable sirs, we do not all agree regarding this matter of various designations.
Let us approach the Blessed One;
having approached him, let us ask the Blessed One about this matter."
"We shall retain it exactly as that Blessed One explains it to us.
Then a great many monks approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, a great number of monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, while we, a great number of monks, were seated and gathered together here in the assembly hall, this kind of conversation arose among us."
"As before, up until: 'We shall retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to us';
thus, Venerable Sir, we ask the Blessed One this very matter: who is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by us?"
As before, up until the point of consuming the foremost alms-food;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, you must honor, revere, respect, and worship the most senior among you."
"One should perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising from one's seat, joining the palms, and respectful conduct;
and he is worthy of receiving from you the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food," so it was said by the Blessed One.
"O householders, you must honor a monk who is more senior [than yourselves]; as before, up until [allowing him] to enjoy the seat of honor."
...and so forth,
are not worthy of veneration.
O monks, they show honor, respect, esteem, and worship to householders who are elders.

Having heard this, the brahmins and householders grumbled, reviled, and spoke in disapproval: "We are noble ones who enjoy sensual pleasures and are submerged in the mire of desire; how can you show us such respect?"
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One; the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I spoke with reference to those who have gone forth, not to householders."
When the monks saw the elders of other sects, they honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped them;
the Blessed One said:
"In this context, I spoke with reference to those who follow the Dharma, but not to outsiders."
Seeing those novice monks who had gone forth at an advanced age, they honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped them.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, I spoke with reference to those who are fully ordained, but not regarding the novices."
They showed respect, honor, esteem, and veneration toward those newly ordained who were senior.
The Blessed One said:
"One should pay homage after having asked each other about the number of years since their full ordination."
When they were asked, they spoke of their years since birth;
the Blessed One said,
"One should ask for the number of years since full ordination."
The monks did not know how many years had passed since their ordination;
the Blessed One said:
"The time [of one's seniority] should be announced."
The monks did not know how many seasonal periods there were;
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, these five are the seasonal periods."
The winter [retreat], the summer [retreat], the rainy [retreat], the short rainy [retreat], and the long rainy [retreat]; therein,
the winter [retreat] consists of four months,
and the summer [retreat] consists of four months.
The annual [retreat] lasts for one month;
the "dying annual" lasts for one day and night;
the "long annual" lasts for three months less one night.
Having thus announced the formal agreement (*sāmāyika*), he who was ordained earlier is to be saluted;
furthermore, four other monks are to be saluted.
Which four are to be saluted?

In this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, including gods and humans, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of veneration; likewise,
all those who have gone forth are worthy of veneration by householders.
Among all those who have received full ordination (*upasaṃpanna*), those ordained earlier are to be venerated by those ordained later, with the exception of a *bhikṣuṇī*;
even if a *bhikṣuṇī* has been ordained for a hundred years, a *bhikṣu* ordained on that very day is to be venerated by her.
Everyone who has not received full ordination must pay homage to one who has received full ordination.
There are ten who are not to be paid homage;
which are the ten?

One undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), one undergoing initial probation (*mūlapārivāsika*), one whose probation has been completed (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*), one undergoing the *mānāpya* penance (*mānāpyacārika*), one who has completed the *mānāpya* (*caritamānāpya*), one suspended for not seeing [an offense] (*adarśanāyotkṣiptaka*), one suspended for not making amends (*apratikarmāyotkṣiptaka*), one suspended for not relinquishing an evil view (*apratinisṛṣṭe pāpake dṛṣṭigate utkṣiptaka*), every householder, and everyone who is not fully ordained (*anupasaṃpanna*)— when these were designated by the Blessed One according to seniority (*yathāvṛddhikayā*), then the monks honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped one another.
Honoring, revering, respecting, and worshiping one another, they flourished in wholesome qualities like a lotus in water.
Then the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, when the Blessed One had prescribed [the rules] according to seniority, then the monks honored, revered, respected, and worshipped one another."
"Honoring, respecting, revering, and worshiping one another, they flourish in wholesome qualities like a lotus in water.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, what is the wonder here that now, by me who am free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion..."

Being liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, he was omniscient, possessed of knowledge of all modes, and had attained mastery over all knowledge and its objects.

When the *yathāvṛddhika* (seniority-based seating) was designated, and having relied upon that *yathāvṛddhika*, the monks honored and revered one another, as previously described, until it was said: "just as the blue lotus [floats] upon the water."

Listen now to how, by me—who was possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion; who was not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; and whose body had fallen into ruin—by means of the seniority that was designated according to age, and by virtue of that seniority, the entire population dwelling in Jambudvīpa was for the most part reborn in the sublime assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The Story of the Francolin Partridge, the Hare, the Monkey, and the Elephant

Long ago, monks, in a certain dense forest in the kingdom of Kāśī, there lived four creatures: a partridge, a hare, a monkey, and an elephant. They dwelt together in friendship, united, harmonious, and in mutual affection; without dispute, free from suspicion, they passed their time living as they pleased.
Then, at another time, an idea occurred to them.
"Sirs, we exist here in mutual friendship, united, harmonious, in agreement, and without dispute;
yet we do not know who among us should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.
What if we were to establish a system according to seniority?"
They began to converse with one another, saying,
"Who among us is the eldest?
Thereupon, Kapiñjala pointed out a banyan tree.
"Sirs, by whom and how large was this banyan tree seen?
The elephant replied, "As I was traveling along this path with my herd, it was seen by me; it is equal to my own height in its elevation."
The monkey said, "As I was traveling along this path with my troop, I saw him; he is exactly equal to me in height.
They replied:
"You are his elder," [the hare said].
The hare replied,
"Even I have licked the drops of dew from the leaves of this two-leaved tree with my tongue."
They said:
"You too are the eldest of these two.
Kapiñjala replied:
"Behold this banyan tree, which has reached a great size.
They replied, "We see it. [He said,] "Having eaten its fruits, I voided my excrement in this spot, and from that this [tree] was born."
They said:
"If that is so, you are the eldest among us all.
Thereupon, the elephant began to show honor to everyone.

The monkey honored the hare and the francolin; the hare likewise honored the francolin; thus, honoring one another according to their seniority, they wandered here and there through that forest thicket.
When uneven and low-lying places had to be traversed, then the monkey would mount the elephant, the hare the monkey, and the partridge the hare;
as their affection and respect for one another thus increased, the thought occurred to them:
"Sirs, we have grown in affection and respect for one another; there is yet more [to be done]. (MSV III 127)
"In that case, let us live having undertaken some wholesome practice.
"What shall we do?
Kapinjala said:
"We shall abstain from taking life.
Of what nature is our taking of life?
Kapiṃjala said:
There are grasses, flowers, and fruits that contain living beings, and there are those that are free of living beings;
therefore, from this day forward, we should abandon those with living beings and consume only those that are free of living beings.
Having abandoned those containing living beings, they began to consume those free from living beings.
Then this thought occurred to them:
"We have desisted from taking life, but we do not yet desist from taking what is not given."
"What constitutes theft for us?
Kapiṃjala replied:
"There are grasses, leaves, flowers, and fruits that have owners, and there are those that have no owners."
"Therefore, from this day forward, we shall abandon those things that involve possessions and enjoy only those that are free from possessions.
Having abandoned those things involving possessions, they began to enjoy only those that were free from possessions.
This occurred to them:
"We are indeed abstaining from taking what is not given, but we are not yet abstaining from sexual misconduct;
what if we were now to abstain from sexual misconduct?"
"What is our sexual misconduct like?
Kapiṃjala replied:
"We have intercourse even with those who are approachable."
"We go even to those who should not be approached;

therefore, from this day forward, we must go only to those who are approachable and not to those who are unapproachable. They went to those who were approachable and not to those who were unapproachable.
Then this thought occurred to them:
"We have indeed abstained from sexual misconduct,
but not from false speech;
what if we were now to abstain from false speech?"
"What kind of false speech do we have?
Kapiṃjala replied:
"We prattle on about this or that."
"Therefore, from this day forward, we must not prattle on about this or that;
rather, having reflected and reflected, speech should be uttered at the proper time.
They did not prattle on about this or that, but rather, having reflected and reflected, they uttered their words at the proper time.
This occurred to them: "We have indeed abstained from false speech, but we have not yet abstained from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants."
"What if we were to abstain from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence?
What, for us, constitutes fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that are the basis for negligence?
Kapiñjala said:
"There are intoxicating fruits and there are non-intoxicating fruits;
therefore, from this day forward, we shall abandon the intoxicating fruits and consume the non-intoxicating fruits.
Having thus abandoned the intoxicating fruits, they began to consume the non-intoxicating fruits.
When they had been established in the five bases of the vow, Kapiṃjala said:
"Sirs, we are now established in the five bases of the vow; what if we were also to establish others in the five bases of the vow?"
They said:
"We shall do so;
who among you will establish it?"
The monkey said,
"I shall establish all the monkeys [in their proper places]";
then the hare said:
"I shall establish all the porcupines and hairy deer," he said;
the elephant replied,
"I shall establish all the elephants, lions, tigers, and leopards."
Kapiṃjala said:
"If it is so, then in brief, those among you who are undisciplined—whether bipeds, quadrupeds, or birds—I shall establish them all in the five bases of the vows.
Then they [went] to the region of Kāśī.
All living beings, even those belonging to the animal realm, were established in the five precepts;
they dwelt in that forest grove with full awareness, moving about as they pleased without harming one another;
and through their power, the god began to send rain at the proper time.
The trees were always laden with flowers and fruit, and the earth was rich with crops;
those humans were seen dwelling together, not harming one another.
The trees were always laden with flowers and fruit, and the earth was rich with crops;
the king said:
"I rule the kingdom according to the Dharma; this is my power," he said.
But the women of the inner apartments, the princes, the ministers, the army commanders, and the merchants and country folk said, "This is our power."
The king reflected:
"All of these say, 'It is my power, it is my power,' yet it is not known whose power it actually is."
Filled with curiosity, he summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them;
they too did not know.
Eventually, there was a park not far from Vārāṇasī.
There dwelt a seer possessing the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*), who was honored, revered, and saluted by the entire body of people living in Vārāṇasī.
Then the king approached that seer, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Great Seer, in my realm all living beings, even those born as animals, dwell without harming one another, remaining conscious and at ease, moving about according to their pleasure."
The god always sends rain at the proper time, the trees are laden with flowers and fruit, and the earth is rich with crops;
therefore, this thought occurred to me: "I shall govern the kingdom according to righteousness."
"This is my power," [he thought].
The women of the inner apartments, the princes, the ministers, the army commanders, and the merchants and country folk perceived: "This is our power."
Therefore, it is not known whose power this is;
my curiosity is great,
and you ought to dispel my doubt.
"Whose power is this?
He replied:
"Great King, this is not your power, nor that of the harem, nor of the princes, nor of the ministers, nor of the army and its vanguard."
It is not for the sake of the merchants and country folk;
rather, four living beings dwell within your realm,
and this is their power.
The king said,
"I shall go and see them";
the seer replied:
"Great King, what is the use of seeing them? Rather, you should adopt and practice that which they have adopted and practice.
"What is it that they have adopted and practice?
"The five bases of the vows."
"Great Seer, what are the five items of the vow?
Great King, they do not deprive living beings of life; they do not take away the property of others."
They do not engage in sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached;
they do not speak falsehoods;
and they do not practice the drinking of intoxicants.
The king said:
"Great Seer, if that is so, I too shall undertake and observe these five precepts.
Thereupon, the king began to undertake and observe the five precepts.
Since the king lived having undertaken the five precepts, the queens also began to live having undertaken the five precepts;
the princes, the ministers, the army officers, and the merchants and country folk likewise began to live having undertaken the five precepts; even those from the neighboring borders [did the same].

The provincial kings heard that King Brahmadatta was living having undertaken the five precepts, together with his harem, princes, ministers, military officers, and the people of the towns and countryside;
and having heard this, they too undertook the five precepts.
Together with the women of the inner apartments, the princes, the ministers, the military commanders, and the merchants and countryfolk, they began to live having undertaken [the vows];
indeed, the entire body of people for the most part began to live having undertaken the five precepts.
At that time, whoever in Jambudvīpa met their end was, upon the dissolution of the body, reborn among the exalted gods of the Thirty-three.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing that the assembly of deities was being filled, spoke again in verse:
"With reverence and deference, they dwell in the forest of asceticism,
practicing the holy life of Kapiṃjala as it is proclaimed throughout the world."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was that partridge at that time, on that occasion, was none other than I myself.
Śāriputra the monk was the hare; Maudgalyāyana the monk was the monkey; and Ānanda was the elephant."

Even then, when I had established the practice of seniority (*yathāvṛddhika*), and by means of that practice of seniority, the entire population dwelling in Jambudvīpa was for the most part reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
and now too, when I have established the practice of seniority, and by means of that practice of seniority, the monks— honoring, respecting, revering, and venerating one another—
increase in wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) like a blue lotus in water.
The Buddha praises the community according to seniority:
"Therefore, monks, dwell with reverence, with deference, and with a sense of awe toward your fellow practitioners—whether they be elders, those of middle standing, or juniors. And why is that?"

Monks, it is impossible that a monk who dwells without respect, without deference, and without being under the sway of fear toward elders, those of middle standing, and juniors, will fulfill the rules of proper conduct (*āsamudācārika-dharma*);
it is impossible that he will fulfill the rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*) without having fulfilled the rules of proper conduct.

Without having fulfilled the qualities of one in training, it is impossible that he will fulfill the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
without fulfilling the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, it is impossible that he will attain final nirvana— such a thing cannot exist.

Monks, to that extent, a monk who dwells with reverence, with deference, and under the influence of fear toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether elders, those of middle standing, or juniors—will fulfill the rules of proper conduct;
this is possible.
Having fulfilled the rules of proper conduct, he will fulfill the rules of training; this is possible.

Having fulfilled the qualities of one in training, he will fulfill the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
It is possible that, having fulfilled the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he will attain final nirvana through non-clinging; this is indeed possible.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way.

"Monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall dwell with reverence, with deference, and under the influence of fear toward our fellow celibates—whether elders, those of middle standing, or juniors. This is the establishment of the monasteries (*vihāra*).
When the five [monks] had been disciplined by the Blessed One, they dwelt in the forest;
while dwelling in the forest, they became prey for lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas.
The Blessed One perceived this:
"Where did the disciples of the previous perfectly enlightened ones establish their dwellings? He saw that it was in the monastery;
the deities also informed the Blessed One in this way.
At that time, there lived in Vārāṇasī a householder named Kalyāṇabhadra.
As his mental continuum was awakened by roots of merit, this thought occurred to him:
"O, would that I might cause a monastery to be built for the disciples of the Blessed One!"
Having risen early in the morning, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As the householder Kalyāṇabhadrika sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma;
having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then the householder Kalyāṇabhadrika rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One:
"If the Blessed One would grant permission, I would have a monastery built for the Blessed One’s disciples.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, householder, I authorize you: build it.
He did not know what kind it should be built as;
the Blessed One said:
If you have a three-winged dwelling constructed, a perfumed chamber (gandhakuṭī) should be built in the center, with two dwellings on each of the two sides;
likewise, in a three-winged [structure], there are nine dwellings;
in a four-winged [structure], [the perfumed chamber] is in the center, facing the gateway-chamber (dvārakoṣṭhaka).
There was a fragrant chamber,
and two cells on either side of the doorway; he did not know how many stories should be constructed.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks' dwellings should be built with five stories, the perfumed chamber with seven stories,
and the turret at the top with seven stories."
For the nuns, however, monasteries with three stories should be constructed;
the perfumed chamber (gandhakuṭi) should have five stories;
and the upper pavilion (bālāgrapotikā) should have five stories.
The Story of Anāthapiṇḍada: His Birth and Marvels.

At that time, there lived in Śrāvastī a householder named Datta, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he had accumulated wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her, and as he was thus playing and enjoying himself...
As he was enjoying himself, after some time his wife became pregnant;
and when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth,
and a boy was born.
When twenty-one days—three times seven—had passed after his birth, an extensive birth festival was held, and the naming ceremony was established.
"What shall be the name of the boy?
the kinsmen asked. They replied:
"This boy is the son of the householder Datta; therefore, let the boy's name be Sudatta. Thus the name Sudatta was established for him. The boy Sudatta was entrusted to eight nurses.
two nurses to carry him on their shoulders, two nurses to provide milk,
and two nurses to clean him.
With two playthings,
he was reared and nourished by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various highly refined articles of sustenance,
growing rapidly like a lotus in a pond.
At a later time, adorned with all his ornaments and seated upon his nurse’s hip, he went outside; there, a beggar requested his ornaments, saying: "Prince, I am in need of these ornaments."
"Give me the ornament," he said;
with a joyful heart, the other gave him the ornament,
and he entered his home.
His father asked his nurse,
"Where is the prince's ornament?
and she replied:
The prince gave it to the petitioner;
he was then adorned with another ornament.
That too was given;
again, it was adorned;
that too was given by him.
That householder addressed his wife:
"My dear, a fine son has been born to us; he is constantly delighted by giving."
She said,
"Noble son, if that is so, I shall not adorn him again. He said:
"Lady, we have immeasurable gold and jewels;
however, there are no craftsmen to fashion ornaments.
Therefore, by no means should this go outside."
"He must be expelled";
yet he was pampered right there inside.
Then, at another time, the householder Datta, surrounded by his servants, [arrived].
Having set out to bathe in the Ajīravatī River,
the boy Sudatta said,
"Father, I am going too."
He began to deceive him, saying:
"Son, right here the water is excellent; the river is infested with crocodiles."
"This nurse will bathe you," he said;
he began to cry,
and his mother spoke to him:
"Noble son, for what reason is this boy crying?
He related the matter exactly as it had happened,
and she said:
"Noble son, let her go with you;
what contradiction is there in this? She will be even more thoroughly protected."
Taking him with him, he went to a river;
having bathed him, he established him in a noble family, who then asked:
"Father, for what reason is my protection being provided?"
"Son, you have a fault; how so? You give away the ornaments given to you to beggars. Does your father need wealth?"
"My son, who is not desirous of wealth? Dear father, if it is so, then take me down.
He was taken down by him.

Then, having immersed both hands in the river, he drew up four iron chests filled with gold; he said, "Father, take as much of this wealth as you require, perform your financial business, and let the remainder float right here.
[The father replied,] "Son, do you see treasures submerged in the water?"
"Father, not only those in the water, but even those on land—whether they have owners or are ownerless, whether they are far away or nearby [he gives them].
With eyes wide open in amazement, the householder Datta reflected:
"It is indeed possible for one with such mastery over giving to bestow gifts. Having understood this, he said:
"Son, if it is so, give gifts as you wish";
for this is the natural law:
a son does not become illustrious as long as his father is still living.
Then, at another time, the householder Datta passed away and Sudatta became the master of the household;
it was widely rumored everywhere that he constantly provided alms-food to the destitute.
The son of the householder Datta became the master of the household, Sudatta;
because he provided alms-food to the destitute, he was known as Anāthapiṇḍada.
The designation "householder" arose;
then he brought a wife from a family of equal status,
and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
As he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him;
in this manner, seven sons were born,
and he provided for the marriage of six of them.
The seventh was named Sujāta;
he sought out a family suitable for him, but did not find one that pleased him.
Placing his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought;
he had a young friend named Madhuskandha,
who saw him thus absorbed in reflection.
He said:
"Householder, why do you stand there lost in thought with your cheek resting on your hand?
He replied:
"I have arranged the marriages for six of my sons;
as for the seventh, Sujāta, I am considering which family would be suitable for him—what family might I choose from to arrange his marriage? He said:
"Remain free from anxiety; I shall search for a family suitable for him.
In which region?
He replied:
"I am going to the Magadha region for now; do so. He then went to Rājagṛha.
In Rājagṛha there was a certain householder, wealthy, of great means and great enjoyment, who was the counterpart of Anāthapiṇḍada;
he entered his house and, standing in the gateway hall, said:
"Hail! Hail!"
His household members said to him:
"Brahmin, what do you seek?
"I seek a girl in marriage."
"For what purpose? [They replied:
"In Śrāvastī there is a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada; his son is named Sujāta.
They say, 'He is our equal by birth.'"
"However, our bride-price is very great.
How great is it?
A hundred horses, a hundred gold coins, a hundred mule-carts, and a hundred Kāmboja maidens."
The young brahmin Madhuskandha sent a letter to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with this message:
having read it, [the householder] replied, "Accept it all; everything shall be given by me."
On account of that conjunction of day and muhūrta, it was consecrated;

then, having been fully satisfied by those men with abundant, pure, and excellent food, the young man went to his hall and retired for rest, but he suffered from choleraic dysentery; these were Brahmins who were strangers to him.
Out of fear of the impurity, they cast him out and discarded him outside;
by chance, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived at that place and saw him.
Then, having scraped him with a bamboo splinter and rubbed him with white clay by those two, he was bathed;
after they had taught him the Dharma, they departed,
and his dysentery did not subside.
Having developed a mind of serene faith toward those two, he passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings;
having approached the presence of the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, he requested a palace.
He said:
"Go; that very Śivikā gate shall be your residence.
Having gone there, he became a resident.
The King of Videha sent a hundred Himalayan elephants as a gift to King Bimbisāra;
that king then sent word to Prasenajit of Kosala:
"The King of Videha has sent me a hundred Himalayan elephants."
"If you are in need of a servant," [the king said].
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached King Prasenajit of Kosala;
having approached, he spoke thus to King Prasenajit of Kosala:
"Your Majesty, I have some business in Rājagṛha;
having gone there, I shall return," he said,
and the king replied:
"It is well; go, and bring a hundred elephants for me as well, so that you may take them back. He replied:
"Your Majesty, if there is a need for me there, I shall take [it]; having come here, I will ascertain Your Majesty's intention. The king said:
"Excellent! Let it be so," [said the Buddha]. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, taking with him a large dowry, went to Rājagṛha.
In whichever householder’s home he has taken up residence, that householder rises early in the night and addresses his household:
"Arise, noble ones, arise!
Friends, split the wood and kindle the sacrificial fire!"
Cook the rice;
cook the soup;
prepare the snacks.
"Prepare the circular arena!
Then, this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"What now, will there be a wedding or a marriage for this householder?"
Has he invited the kingdom to a meal?
Or a guild, or a corporation, or an assembly? Or has he invited King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha to a meal?
Having understood this, he said to that householder:

"Householder, is there perhaps a marriage to be celebrated for you, or a wedding? Or have you invited the kingdom to a meal? Or a guild, or a corporation, or an assembly? Or has the King of Magadha, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, been invited by you to a meal?"
He said:

"Householder, there will be no wedding for me, nor a marriage; nor have I invited the kingdom to a meal, nor a guild, nor a corporation, nor an assembly, nor even has King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited to a meal. Rather, the community of monks with the Buddha at its head has been invited to a meal."

Thus, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard this sound of "Buddha," the likes of which he had never heard before, all the pores of his skin bristled with joy. With his hair standing on end, he said this to that householder:
"Householder, who is this called 'Buddha'?"

"Householder, there is a śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, out of perfect faith, from the home into the homeless state."
He has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
he, O householder, is what is called a Buddha.
And who, O householder, is what is called the Saṅgha?

"Householder, there are sons of good family who, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes, have gone forth from the home to the homeless life out of perfect faith, following that very Blessed One who has himself gone forth— whether they be from a kṣatriya family,
or from a brāhmaṇa family, or from a vaiśya family, or even from a śūdra family."
Having donned saffron-colored robes, with perfect faith they went forth from the home to the homeless life, following after that very Blessed One who had gone forth;
this, householder, is what is called the Saṅgha.
"Tomorrow I have invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a meal at my home.
Householder, where does the Blessed One reside at present?
"In this very city of Rājagṛha, in the Śītavana cemetery."
"Householder, is it possible for us to see that Blessed One? "In that case, householder, wait for a moment; it is possible that you will see him here tomorrow once he has arrived."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having fallen asleep that night with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha,
approached the Śivaka Gate at the hour of dawn while perceiving it to be day.
At that time, the Śivaka Gate remained open during two watches of the night.
"Let there be no obstacle for the messengers coming from the east and the west, nor for those going away";
and he saw that the gate of Śivaka was open and filled with light.
This occurred to him: "Surely the night has turned to dawn,
for the gate of Śivaka stands wide open."
Having understood this, he went out from the city by that very light;
and as soon as he had gone out, that light disappeared.
Darkness appeared;
he was seized by fear;
he was overcome with trembling.
His hair stood on end with horror,
thinking, "May no human or non-human, no rogue, or no one at all cause me harm, lest this abundant bride-price remain unpaid.
Having realized this and desiring to turn back, he circumambulated the sacrificial ground of the divine son Madhuskandha.
And he paid homage.
Then, this thought occurred to the divine son Madhuskandha:
"Today, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada must attain the vision of the Truth."

"Thinking, 'This very day he will abandon the Buddha, the Blessed One, and pay homage to another deity,' [the Buddha], having perceived this, illuminated the space from the Śivaka Gate as far as the Śītavana cemetery with a sublime radiance, and addressed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
'Come forward, householder!'"
Do not retreat;
for you, advancing will be better than retreating.
For what reason?
A hundred horses, a hundred gold coins, a hundred mule-carts filled with various kinds of wealth,
and a hundred mare-carts.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single step taken [toward the Buddha].
Come forward, householder;
do not retreat. For you, it is better to advance.
He does not turn back.
For what reason?
Because there are a hundred Himalayan elephants, adorned with gold and jewels.
Elephant-kings with tusks like plow-poles, massive in body and well-trained, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the value of a single step taken by [the Buddha].
Advance, householder; do not retreat;
for one who advances—*abhikrāmataḥ*.
For them, it is better; it does not lead to regression.
Why is that?
A hundred maidens from Kāmboja, adorned with jeweled earrings,
wearing golden armlets, with gold coins upon their necks, and beautifully decorated— even they are not worth a sixteenth part of a single step taken in pilgrimage.
Come forward, householder;
do not retreat. For you who come forward, it will be better.
He did not turn back;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to that son of the gods: "Who are you, noble sir?"
"Householder, I am a young brahmin named Madhuskandha;

I was formerly an old friend of yours. Having conceived a serene faith in the minds of the two monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, I have passed away and been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."
He is a resident right here at this very gateway of Śivikā;
therefore, I say to you: "Go forward, householder, do not turn back."
"It is better for you to go forward than to turn back";
then this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
The Buddha will not be inferior, nor will his teaching of the Dharma be inferior,
since even the deities now apply themselves with zeal to behold that Blessed One.
Having understood this, he went toward the Śītavana cemetery.
At that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth on a walkway in the open air outside the monastery, for the most part waiting for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the Blessed One from afar;
having seen him, he approached the Blessed One,
and having approached, the householder greeted the Blessed One with words of salutation.
"Is the Blessed One sleeping in comfort?
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"In every way, indeed, the brahmin who has attained final nirvāṇa sleeps in comfort. (Śay-v 17)
For he who is liberated and free from acquisitions is not defiled by desires.
Having cut through all attachments here and subdued the fever of the heart,
one who is tranquil sleeps happily with a mind that has attained peace.
Then the Blessed One, taking the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with him, entered the monastery and sat down on the prepared seat.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
He gladdens them;
he gives a Dharma discourse that is appropriate for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to be delivered at the outset, namely:

a discourse on generosity, a discourse on ethical conduct, a discourse on heaven; and, in detail, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, their disadvantages, and their defilement; as well as the benefits of renunciation and seclusion, and the factors conducive to purification.

And when the Blessed One saw that his mind was joyful, pliant, glad, and free from hindrances, and that he was capable and competent to understand the preeminent teaching of the Dharma, then he fully proclaimed in detail that preeminent teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—namely, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Then, while seated on that very seat, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada realized the Four Noble Truths.
Namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains and ready for dyeing, would properly take the color when placed in the dye, even so did the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, while seated on that very seat, realize the four noble truths.
Namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma—having crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, being independent of others and no longer led by others, having attained fearlessness regarding the teachings in the Teacher’s instruction—rose from his seat and draped his upper robe over one shoulder.
Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, he said this to the Blessed One: "I have transcended, Venerable Sir, I have transcended! I go for refuge to the Blessed One."

"Please accept me as a lay follower who, from this day forward for as long as life lasts, has gone for refuge with full confidence, endowed with my very life-breath— to the Dharma and to the Saṅgha of monks.
Then the Blessed One said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"What is your name, householder?
"I am, venerable sir, Sudatta by name;
however, I provide alms-food to those who are without protectors."
Therefore, people recognize me as "the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
"Householder, from what region do you come?
"Venerable sir, there is a town of the Kosalans named Śrāvastī in the eastern provinces."
I dwell there.
May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī; Anāthapiṇḍada invites the Buddha to Śrāvastī.
"I shall attend upon the Blessed One for as long as I live with robes, almsfood, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of monks.
Householder, are there monasteries in Śrāvastī?
"No, venerable sir."
"Householder, wherever monasteries exist, there monks consider it appropriate to come, to go, and to reside.
Let the Blessed One come;
I shall act in such a way that monasteries will be established in Śrāvastī."
"The monks will think that they must come, go, and stay [here].
The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Blessed One had consented through his silence, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.
Then, having performed and accomplished all that was his business or duty in Rājagṛha, he approached the Blessed One once more;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, grant me a monk as a companion, with whom I may have a companion to build a monastery for the sake of the Blessed One in Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One reflected:
"Of which monk is the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, along with his retinue and the populace residing in Śrāvastī, under the influence?
He saw that it was the monk Śāriputra;
thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Pay attention, Śāriputra, to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada together with his retinue, and to the body of people residing in Śrāvastī.
The venerable Śāriputra consented to the Blessed One by remaining silent.
Then the venerable Śāriputra, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then,
at the end of that very night, the venerable Śāriputra dressed in the forenoon,
took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Having walked for alms in Rājagṛha and finished his meal, and having returned from his alms-round after the meal, he put away his bedding as it had been used, took up his bowl and robe,
and set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, taking with him abundant provisions for the journey, reached Śrāvastī by staying one night at each stage.
As soon as he entered Śrāvastī, walking from grove to grove, from park to park, from garden to garden, and pacing back and forth, he wandered about and said this:
"Which spot of ground will be not too far from Śrāvastī?"

"Not too near, with few people during the day and little noise at night, with little sound and little clamor, and with little contact from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles— there I shall have a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw it.

The park of Prince Jeta was neither too far from Śrāvastī nor too near; it was quiet during the day, with little clamor, and at night it had little noise, little sound, and little disturbance from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and crawling reptiles.
Upon seeing this, the thought occurred to him:
"I shall have a monastery built here for the sake of the Blessed One."
As soon as he had entered his own residence, he approached Prince Jeta;
having approached him, he said this to Prince Jeta:
"Prince, grant me the grove."
"I shall have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One.
He replied,
"Householder, that park does not belong to me."
"But that garden belongs to me.
A second and even a third time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to Prince Jeta:
"Prince, please grant me the park."
"I shall have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One.
"The park has not been relinquished by me, householder, even for a covering of ten million pieces of gold.
Again, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the youth Jeta:
"You have paid the price for the grove, O prince;
accept the gold and bullion;
the grove is mine."
"Who has received the guest-offering?
"You have received it.
They fell into a dispute, saying, "I have received it, you have not received it."
They set out toward where the lay officials were.
In the meantime, this thought occurred to the four world-protectors:
"This householder Anāthapiṇḍada is intent on having a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One."
"Assistance must be rendered to him"; thereupon, having manifested themselves as judicial officers, they sat down in the court of justice.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada and Prince Jeta approached the judicial officials;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada explained this matter in detail to the judicial officers,
and they said:
"You have been offered the price for the grove, O prince; accept this gold,
[and let it be] a park for the community of monks."
He remained silent;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having brought out abundant gold by means of carts, loads, baskets, boxes, camels, oxen, and donkeys,
began to cover the entire Jeta Grove with it.
It was not finished;
some portion of the ground remained uncovered.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, reflecting on this matter, stood silent for a moment.
What will that treasure be like?
It shall be neither too small nor too large, such that this uncovered portion of the earth will be covered by it.
"Furthermore, it will not need to be guarded.
Prince Jeta reflected:
"Surely the householder Anāthapiṇḍada has come to regret [his gift]."
"Knowing, 'Why should I relinquish such a vast heap of wealth for the sake of a grove? he said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
'Householder, if you have regret, take back the gold.'"
"This is my very own pleasure grove;
I have no regret, O prince.
However, reflecting upon this very matter, I remained silent for a moment."
What will that treasure be like?
It shall be neither too small nor too large,
by which this uncovered portion of the earth will be covered.
"And furthermore, he will not need to be guarded.
Then this thought occurred to Prince Jeta:
"Surely the Buddha will not be an inferior one!"
"The proclamation of the Dharma is not insignificant, since this householder now relinquishes such a vast heap of wealth for the sake of a park.
Having understood this, he said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, grant me a portion of ground not yet covered;
there I shall have a gateway constructed for the sake of the Blessed One.
Anāthapiṇḍada the householder then granted Prince Jeta a portion of ground not yet covered.
Where Prince Jeta was having a gateway constructed for the sake of the Blessed One— now,

as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had begun to have a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One, the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthyas), their minds agitated by intense hatred, gathered together and went to where Anāthapiṇḍada was.
The householders approached him;
having approached, they said:
"Householder, do not have a monastery built here for the sake of the ascetic Gautama."
What is the reason? We have divided the cities among ourselves; Rājagṛha belongs to the ascetic Gautama.
"Śrāvastī is ours";
he replied,
"The cities have already been divided by you."
"But this is not my private property;
I shall have a pillar of Dharma erected for whomever so desires.
They then went into the presence of the king.
There too they were defeated by Anāthapiṇḍada;
the heretics, like crows with unaltered faces, said:
"Householder, we do not grant you your wish."
"The foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama has arrived;
if he defeats us in debate,
then have a monastery built."
He said, "Excellent; let me first seek the consent of the noble Śāriputra.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Śāriputra and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, the non-Buddhist teachers say this:"
"Householder, we do not grant you the freedom to act as you wish;
the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama has arrived.
If he defeats us in debate,"
"Have a monastery built";
"How should one proceed in this matter?
Venerable Śāriputra reflected.
"Are there any roots of merit in these people, or are there none? He sees that there are; "To whom are they bound?
To me alone."
Again he reflects:
"Are these alone my disciples bound to me for training, or are there others also who are to be trained by means of debate? He sees that there are;
he considers: "After how long will they assemble? (Śay-v 24)
He sees that it will be after seven days have passed; having reflected, he says:
"Householder, let this be so for him; what [is the use of further deliberation]?"
On the seventh day,
the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, filled with joy and gladness, approached the non-Buddhist teachers; having approached them, he spoke thus to the non-Buddhist teachers:
The Venerable Ārya Śāriputra said: "Excellent;
let it be so; however, on the seventh day."
They reflected:
"There must be one of two reasons for this;
either he wishes to flee."
Or perhaps he wishes to seek out an ally;
what is appropriate for this occasion?
We too shall seek out an ally.
They began to search for an ally;
while they were searching for an ally, they saw a wandering mendicant named Raktākṣa,
and they spoke to him.
"You are our fellow practitioner of the holy life; you, the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama, have been challenged by us to debate, and he is now searching for an ally."
"Provide us with your assistance;
after how much time? "On the seventh day from now. "Excellent."
"So be it;
whenever an assembly of yours takes place, you must inform me.
The heretics, their minds filled with suspicion and agitation, are searching for a flaw day after day."
The non-Buddhists (*tīrthya*) and Śāriputra counted the days as they vied with one another,
until on the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had seats prepared upon a vast expanse of ground.
A lion-throne was prepared for the venerable Śāriputra;
non-Buddhist teachers dwelling in various regions had assembled;
as had the populace residing in Śrāvastī and many hundreds of thousands of living beings dwelling in its vicinity.
Some had come out of curiosity,
while others were impelled by their previous roots of merit;
then the Venerable Śāriputra, escorted and surrounded by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his retinue, [entered] the circle of debaters.
Having entered and surveyed those to be trained, he ascended the lion throne with a smile and a perfectly peaceful deportment and sat down.
The entire assembly sat down, their minds attentive, gazing intently at the Venerable Śāriputra.
[The Defeat of the Tīrthyas]
Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the non-Buddhist teachers: "Sirs, will you first construct [the hall],
or will you dismantle it?"
They said:
"We shall do it; you transform yourself."
The Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"If I were to perform it, even the world with its gods would not be able to undo it."
Knowing that the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa was already there, he said this to the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa: "You do it;
I shall transform it."
He was skilled in the art of illusion;
by him, a mango tree in full bloom was conjured up.
Then, by the Venerable Śāriputra, a violent wind and rain were summoned.
It was cast away; having been uprooted along with its very roots, it was scattered here and there until it became beyond the reach even of practitioners of yoga.
Then, by him, a lotus pond was created;
by the Venerable Śāriputra, a young elephant was created.
He crushed her on all sides;
he then manifested a seven-headed nāga;
the Venerable Śāriputra manifested a garuḍa.
By whomsoever he was carried off,
by him a vetāḍa was conjured up;
the Venerable Śāriputra pinned it down with mantras.
A Vetāla, when wrongly employed, intends its own destruction;
it rushed right upon him.
Thereupon, terrified, trembling, agitated, and with the hair on his body standing on end, he fell at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra.
"Noble Śāriputra, protect me! I have come to you for refuge.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra neutralized the spells, and that vetāḍa was pacified.
The Venerable Śāriputra taught him the Dharma; having conceived faith, he said:
"Noble Śāriputra, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
"I shall practice the holy life in the presence of the venerable Śāriputra.
The venerable Śāriputra ordained him, conferred full admission upon him, and gave him instruction.
By striving, exerting himself, and making an effort, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

He became an Arhat; free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the super-knowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights, turned away from existence, gain, and desire, he became one worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
Then that assembly, their eyes wide with wonder,
became filled with faith toward the Venerable Śāriputra and said:
"The Great Noble Śāriputra has subdued the bull among debaters!"
Having understood this, they turned their gaze toward the face of the Venerable Śāriputra.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, having discerned the inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of that assembly,
delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, upon hearing which many thousands of beings—
A great distinction has arisen:
some have generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, and some for pratyekabuddha enlightenment.
Some [set their minds] upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
some took up the precepts of going for refuge;
and some realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Some attained the fruit of once-returning;
some the fruit of non-returning;
and some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the complete abandonment of all afflictions.
For the most part, that assembly was inclined toward the Buddha,
leaning toward the Dharma,
and tending toward the Saṅgha.
[The matter] was settled;
the non-Buddhist teachers reflected:
"It is not possible for us to defeat him in debate."
"A stratagem must be devised:
let us work here for wages;
then, having found an opportunity, we shall have him killed by a hired assassin."
They all went together to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and said,
"Householder, you have cut off all our means of livelihood; therefore, please show us compassion."
"We shall perform work for hire in your monastery;
we have resided here for a long time, so let us not abandon this country."
Anāthapiṇḍada said,
"I shall first seek the venerable Śāriputra";
he then approached where the venerable Śāriputra was.
Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Noble one,
the heretics say..."
They said,
"All our means of livelihood have been cut off by you;
therefore, please show us compassion."
"We shall perform work for hire in your monastery;
we have resided here for a long time,
so let us not abandon this region."
The Venerable Śāriputra began to reflect:
"Do they possess any roots of merit, or do they not? He saw that they did possess them; he then considered with whom those roots were connected.
Thinking, "It shall be mine alone," he reflects and says:
"Householder, let it be so."
"What contradiction is there in this? they thought, and so they began to perform labor for wages in that monastery;
then the Venerable Śāriputra manifested a fierce man as a supervisor of the workmen.
He began to have that work performed;
the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing it was the time for their conversion, stood walking back and forth near them at the foot of a tree,
and he was seen by them.
They reflected,
"This is the time to kill him, for he stands in a secluded place";
they approached him and stood surrounding him.
The Venerable Śāriputra reflected: "With what kind of mind have these approached me? and he saw that it was with a murderous intent.
By him, that created vine-guard was released;
by him they were pursued with the words, "Go! Perform your work!
They replied:
"Noble Śāriputra, save me! He replied, "Venerable one, go."
"Let them rest for now," he said;
they reflected,
"Such is this Great-Souled One."
"Thinking, 'We have murderous intentions toward him,
whereas he has a mind of loving-kindness toward us,' they became full of faith.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, having understood their underlying tendencies, latent dispositions, elements, and natures, [taught] a discourse conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths."

A teaching on the Dharma was given, hearing which they shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
(The Conversion of the Tīrthikas)
Having seen the truths, they said: "Śāriputra, may we receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
may we, O Venerable Śāriputra, practice the holy life under you."
They were ordained and received full admission by the Venerable Śāriputra; instruction was given to them, and as they applied themselves, [they practiced].

By striving and exerting themselves, having understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra as unstable and shifting, and having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, perishing, scattering, and destruction, they realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.

Thus they became Arhats; free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with minds like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance through knowledge,

having attained the superknowledges, the higher cognitions, and the analytical insights, they turned their backs on existence, gain, greed, and honor, [becoming objects of veneration] for the gods including Indra and Upendra.
They became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation.
There, the Venerable Śāriputra took up the measuring-line for the monastery in a secluded spot.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada also took hold of him by one side;
the Venerable Śāriputra began to manifest a smile,
and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"Noble Śāriputra, Tathāgatas or the disciples of the Tathāgata do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Noble Śāriputra, what is the cause? What is the condition for manifesting this smile?"
"It is so, householder, it is so. Tathāgatas or the disciples of a Tathāgata do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition. And you have here taken up this sutra."
In the Tuṣita host of gods, a golden palace had appeared;
thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, his eyes wide with wonder, said:
"Noble Śāriputra, if it is so,"
"In that case, spread the cloth again even more extensively;
I wish to clarify my mind.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra took up that cloth.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s mind was further purified by an even more intense surge of serene faith;
immediately upon the arising of that faith, that golden mansion was transformed into one made of the four precious gems,
and this was reported to him by the Venerable Śāriputra.
Then, by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, whose succession of merit had increased ever further, sixteen great monasteries were constructed, as well as sixty sites for small cells.
Having built the sixteen great monasteries and the sixty sites for small cells, and having filled them with all necessary requisites, he approached the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached, he said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, by how many stages of travel does the Blessed One proceed on the road?
It is just as, householder, for a wheel-turning monarch."
"What is the distance traveled by a wheel-turning monarch per day?
"Ten *krośas*, householder; a wheel-turning monarch travels the road in ten-day stages.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada calculated the number of halting places along the route between Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha and had rest-houses constructed.
A hall for giving was constructed; a man was appointed to announce the time;
and archways were erected, adorned with parasols, banners, and flags, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and hung with censers of fragrant incense.
Medicines to be taken at specific times and those to be taken at intervals have been prepared. (The messenger to the Buddha)
Then, having gathered the necessary provisions, he addressed a certain man:
"Come, my good man; go to where the Blessed One is."

Having approached, pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One in our name, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, vigor, well-being, strength, blamelessness, and his dwelling in comfort; and speak thus:
"May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One for as long as life lasts,
together with the community of monks, with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
"Very well, noble sir," that man replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and set out for Rājagṛha.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Rājagṛha;
then, having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side;
standing to one side, that man said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One."
As before, up to "and a state of dwelling in comfort";
"May you be happy, O man, as well as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
"Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada says this:"
"May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, for as long as life lasts, providing robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The Blessed One consented to that man by remaining silent.
Then that man, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
Then the Blessed One— tamed, with a retinue of the tamed— arrived at Śrāvastī.
He is peaceful, with a peaceful retinue;
liberated, with a liberated retinue; comforted, with a comforted retinue.
He is disciplined and has a disciplined retinue; he is an Arhat and has a retinue of Arhats;
he is free from passion and has a retinue free from passion.
He was gracious, surrounded by a gracious retinue;
like a bull surrounded by a herd of cows,
like an elephant surrounded by its calves.
Like a lion surrounded by a pack of fanged beasts, like a swan surrounded by a flock of swans,
like a garuḍa surrounded by a host of birds.

Like a brahmin surrounded by a host of disciples, like a skilled physician surrounded by a host of patients, like a hero surrounded by a host of warriors, like a guide surrounded by a host of travelers,
like a caravan leader surrounded by a host of merchants, like a guild master surrounded by his retinue, and like a provincial king surrounded by a host of ministers.
Like a universal monarch surrounded by a thousand sons, like the moon surrounded by the host of stars, like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays,

like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas, like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas, like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas, like Dhanada surrounded by a host of yakṣas, and like Vemacitrin surrounded by a host of asuras—

Like Śakra surrounded by the host of the Thirty-three, like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahma-kāyika gods, like the ocean at rest, like a rain-cloud filled with water, like a lordly elephant free from rut, he— with his senses well-subdued and his deportment and movements undisturbed—
was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

Adorned with the eighty secondary marks, his body radiant, his form graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns— like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides, endowed with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion—
he was accompanied by the community of monks and by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada together with his retinue, the inhabitants of Śrāvastī.
Followed by a great multitude of people and many hundreds of thousands of deities, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One, entering the city of Śrāvastī, deliberately placed his right foot upon the threshold of the city gate, the earth shook in six ways: this great earth trembled, trembled violently, and trembled intensely.
It trembles, it trembles violently, it trembles intensely;
the eastern quarter rises while the western sinks,
and the western rises while the eastern sinks.
The south rises and the north sinks;
the north rises and the south sinks;
the edge rises;
The center sank down; the center rose up while the edges sank down;
and this entire world, together with the intermediate spaces between worlds, became suffused with a sublime radiance in the sky.

And celestial drums resounded; the deities stationed in the expanse of the sky began to scatter divine blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), and great white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) over the Blessed One from above, as well as powdered aloe-wood, saffron powder, *tamāla* leaves,
and divine *māndāraka* flowers, and they waved their garments.
Upon the Blessed One’s entry into the city, these and other such wonders occurred:
narrow places became wide, low places became high, and high places became level; elephants trumpeted, horses neighed, bulls bellowed, and various [instruments] within the houses [resounded].
Musical instruments resound of their own accord;
the blind regain their sight, the deaf their hearing, and the mute become capable of speech;
those with impaired remaining faculties recover their senses.
Those intoxicated by liquor become sober; those who have been made to drink poison become free from poison;
and those who are mutual enemies attain loving-kindness.
Pregnant women give birth safely;
those bound in fetters are released;
and the destitute obtain wealth.
And these and other hundreds of thousands of wonders appeared when the Blessed One entered the city. Then, with such great honor, the Blessed One entered Śrāvastī at the Jetavana.
Having entered, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, surrounded by his friends, kinsmen, and relatives, [carried] a golden [bowl].
Taking up the water-pitcher, he began to pour a stream of water, but it did not fall;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, being dejected, reflected:
"Could it be that I have performed some flawed actions?
The Blessed One said, "Householder, you have not performed any flawed actions; rather, while standing in this very spot, you offered this place to the former Perfectly Awakened Ones."
"Stand in another place and drop it";
he stood in another place and dropped it;
the Blessed One himself proclaimed the Jetavana with a voice endowed with five qualities.
While the name of Jetavana was being proclaimed, Prince Jeta thought to himself, "Oh, would that the Blessed One would mention my name first!
The Blessed One, knowing the mind of Prince Jeta with his own mind, mentioned him first.
"Monks, this Jeta Grove is the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Upon hearing this, Prince Jeta was filled with exceeding faith, thinking, "The Blessed One has mentioned my name first of all.
With a heart born of joy and gladness, he had a gateway pavilion made of the four precious substances constructed for the sake of the Blessed One, using all that wealth.
Likewise, it was recorded in the Sūtra by the Elder compilers: "The Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then the monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: [regarding] the previous births of Anāthapiṇḍada during the time of the seven Buddhas.

"Venerable sir, where was this site of earth previously offered by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to former perfectly enlightened Buddhas? Therefore, having purchased this site from the prince by covering it with six *krośas* of gold and bullion, he offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin.

accompanied by a retinue of sixty thousand monks, he arrived at this very spot.

He covered this area of ground for two and a half krośas with jewels, purchased it from the prince, and offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One Śikhin together with his community of disciples.

Accompanied by a retinue of sixty thousand bhikṣus, he arrived at this place.
At that time, there was a householder named Māghu;
having purchased this site for two krośas from the prince by covering it with pearls, he offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One Viśvabhū together with his community of disciples.
"Monks, it may be that you think, 'At that time, on that occasion, was he perhaps some other householder named Māgha?

Prior to that, in this Bhadraka Kalpa, a teacher named Krakutsunda appeared in the world, as previously described, up until: he was a Buddha, a Blessed One;

the Blessed One; he, accompanied by a retinue of thirty thousand monks, arrived at this very spot.

Accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand, he arrived at this location.
At that time, there was a householder named Āṣāḍha,
who covered half a *krośa* of this ground with golden *yava*-grains.
Having ransomed him from the prince, he was presented to Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, together with his community of disciples.
Monks, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the householder named Āṣāḍha was someone else;

I too have arrived at this place with a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty.

Now, O monks, having been purchased from Prince Jeta by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada through a carpet spread with sixteen ploughs’ worth of gold coins, it shall belong to me and my community of disciples.

At that time, there will arise a householder named Sudhana;
he too, having covered this region for three *yojanas* with gold and bullion, will purchase it from the prince and offer it to Maitreya together with his community of disciples.
Having gone forth in that very teaching, through the abandonment of all afflictions, he will realize the state of an Arhat.
"Monks, it may be that you think, 'At that time, on that occasion, he who was the householder named Sudhana was someone else.

rather, it was this very Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder, who appeared at that time as the householder named Sudhana."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has the power to see hidden treasures,
whether they are near or far, belonging to an owner or ownerless, situated on land or in water— those that are distant as well as those that are close at hand.

A report spread throughout the vicinity: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada perceives treasures—both those with owners and those without owners, both those situated on land and those situated in water, whether they be far away or near.

"Friends, endowed with what characteristic does the householder Anāthapiṇḍada perceive treasures— whether they have an owner or are ownerless, whether they are situated on land or in water, and whether they are far away or near?"

"After reflecting, I shall tell you by what characteristic the householder Anāthapiṇḍada perceives treasures— whether they have an owner or are ownerless, whether they are situated on land or in water, and whether they are far away or near."

Intent on searching for the movements and dwellings of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, he followed closely behind him until, at another time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had finished bathing in the river Ajiravatī and emerged;

"Those who are far away as well as those who are near";
