and the boasting non-Buddhists also informed everyone everywhere.
The news spread among the neighbors:
"Now the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is endowed with such patience and gentleness that he can see treasures—
whether they have an owner or are ownerless, whether they are on land or in water, and whether they are far away or near."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not easy for even hundreds of thousands of millions of non-Buddhist teachers to understand by what characteristic one is endowed [with such qualities]."

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada does not merely see treasures; rather, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada has a treasury variegated with jewels and is a lord of gold by which he sees treasures— whether they have an owner or no owner,
whether they are situated on land or in water, and whether they are far away or near at hand.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the ripening of which resulted in his having a treasury variegated with jewels and becoming a lord of gold?
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the actions performed and accumulated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element."
Neither in the fire element nor in the wind element, but rather only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do the actions performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen;
for actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons.
"Having obtained the collection of conditions and the [proper] time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
(Śay-v 32) The Story of the Pratyekabuddha (Concerning a Previous Life of Anāthapiṇḍada):

Monks, in the past, in a certain mountain village, there lived a householder who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments; his acquisitions were extensive and wide-ranging, and he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa.

When the spring season had arrived, and the forest groves were in full bloom, resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and pheasants, he went out to the pleasure gardens together with his retinue.

At a time when Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise—beings who have compassion for the lowly and the destitute, who delight in remote lodgings and dwellings, and who are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Now, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that mountain village.
He stood in a certain place within that garden;
the gardener informed the householder, saying,
"In this place stands a wandering ascetic of peaceful mind."
Upon hearing this, joy arose within him;
thinking, "I am fortunate that such a renunciant resides in my park," he set out with a mind full of faith to see him.
However, that Great Being had already entered the realm of nirvana without remainder and passed away.
Then that householder, together with his friends, relatives, kinsmen, and household members, cremated him with great honor;
that pyre was extinguished with milk;
and those bones were mixed with jewels and placed in a jar made of crystal.
Those [bones] appeared to be situated inside [the chest], and they emitted sounds;
then, having prostrated at his feet, he made this aspiration:
"Just as these bones of his, interspersed with jewels, shine exceedingly and emit sounds, may I likewise, through this root of merit, have a chest variegated with jewels and become a lord of gold."
What do you think, monks?
That householder at that time and on that occasion was none other than this very householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Because he performed a service for the pratyekabuddha and made a vow, as did the householder Tiṣya—
Being the nephew of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, he placed a jewel upon the stupa of Vipaśyin’s hair and nails, which was composed of light;
as the ripening of that karma, he became possessed of a treasure-chest variegated with jewels and a lord of gold.

Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

having abandoned black deeds and those that are mixed, one should apply oneself exclusively to deeds that are entirely white. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. This is the intermediate summary verse.
Tiṣya, Puṣya, Māghu, Bhavadatta, Bṛhaspati,
Āṣāḍha, Sudatta, and Sudhana shall be the last.
Gold, fine gold, and pearls as the third;
with cows, cloths, and barley, ten million was raised in gold.

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having spread out a layer of crores [of gold pieces], purchased [the park] from Prince Jeta and offered it to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, then the faithful inhabitants of various countries...
Those who go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the caityas—
some among them, being full of faith, say: "Noble one, we too would have some building constructed for the noble Saṅgha in Jeta’s Grove— should we do so?"
—thus [he said]. The monks said:
"Buy the ground with a price and have it built.
[The patron asked: "Noble one, for what price is it given?"
"With so much gold?
"Noble sir, from where would we get that much?
Nevertheless, if we can obtain it in this region, we shall have it made."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"The householder should be consulted."
"If he permits it, it should be built";
the monks looked toward the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,
and he said:

"Having come to me, faithful brahmins and householders perform bases of meritorious action for the sake of the Saṅgha; I authorize this. They perform them for the sake of an individual; I do not authorize this.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that it may be built for the sake of the Saṃgha;
for the sake of an individual, the donor must be consulted."
If he grants permission, it should be carried out; if he does not grant permission,
it should not be carried out.
Some visiting monks, having come to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the caitya,
entered among the resident monks according to their social connections;
they were friends with some of them.
They do not exist [therein] and they are not frustrated;
regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"For the sake of newcomers, an unassigned object should be set aside."
In a certain mountain hamlet there was a monastery; there the monks entered the rains retreat.
When a danger arose in that small town during the rainy season, the monks residing there became terrified; not having been invited to stay, they came to Śrāvastī.
Having been accommodated by the resident monks and once their fatigue from the journey had been dispelled, they said:
"Venerable ones, assign the lodgings.
They did not assign them, thinking, "It is during the rainy season.
The visiting monks criticized, reviled, and complained about this.
"How is it now, venerable ones, that you cause the teaching of the Teacher who is still present to disappear? If you have any remorse, assign the lodgings according to seniority!
Even so, they did not assign them.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin story, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that a second invitation for the rains retreat (varṣopanāyikā) should be performed for the sake of those monks who have broken their vows or whose vows are shattered."
The monks did not know how it should be performed;
the Blessed One said:

"The invitation (*pravāraṇā*) should be performed after three months, but the second rainy-season retreat (*varṣopanāyikā*) should be performed in the month of Śrāvaṇa. Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"For the sake of those monks whose [robes] have been torn apart, the second rainy-season retreat should be performed."
Meanwhile, other monks who had been defeated by various means also arrived at Śrāvastī;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:

"O monks, it was on account of the monks who were broken by various stratagems that I prescribed a second invitation for the rains-retreat, but not a third. Those monks who were broken by various stratagems should be given rest according to their acquaintance with others.
Yet those monks cause them to perform manual labor."
The Blessed One said:
"They must not be made to undertake [monastic] duties";
yet the monks continued to provide them with their gains.
The Blessed One said: "No gain should be given to them";
even the monks did not provide them with material gains.
The Blessed One said:
"They have obtained material gains, but not robes. Thereupon, the faithful caused many monasteries to be built.
In Śrāvastī, few monks had entered the rains retreat;
they remained in empty dwellings, so that the donors did not obtain merit resulting from the use [of their gifts].
They were being inhabited by sons of Māra;
the Blessed One said:
"All should be assigned—two, three, or four to each one according to their capacity—and all should be used."
In some cases one should remain during the forenoon, in some at midday, and in others in the afternoon.
"One must stay somewhere during the night";
however, those monks did not perform the ritual action and were distracted;
the Blessed One said:
The donor should be encouraged; if he succeeds in providing them, that is well;
if he does not succeed, they should be supplied from the property of the Saṃgha.
"If it is not possible [to perform the ritual for all], then the consecration (saṃskāra) must be performed for as many as is possible,
while the others are to be overlooked.
When this became widespread from the Blessed One, many monks arrived at Śrāvastī.
They were troubled regarding the dwelling place.
The Blessed One said:

"It should be assigned for two or three people; at the very least, it should be assigned for all of them collectively, with a seating area of sufficient size, and a place for the water jar, drinking water, medicine, tooth-sticks, and bowls."
The Blessed One has stated that while mutual courtesy and formal etiquette are indeed common, they should not be specifically prescribed [as a rule];

rather, [one should frequent] various forest retreats, the roots of trees, empty dwellings, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, woods, and wilderness tracts. (Śay-v 36)
Meditate, monks, on remote lodgings;
do not be negligent.
"Lest you later come to regret it"; thus,
the excellence of dwelling in the wilderness was praised in many ways,
and at that time some monks, having undertaken the practice of living in the wilderness, settled in the forest.
There they were robbed by thieves;
having been robbed, while seeking robes from the families of brahmins and householders, they neglected their instruction, recitation, study, yoga, and mental attention.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"A dwelling place should be established for the sake of forest-dwelling monks";
thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
"A dwelling place should be established for the sake of the forest-dwelling monks.
The monks established it in a concealed location.
A forest-dwelling monk, having set down his bowl and robes and closed the door, took his staff and departed.
An affliction arose for those forest-dwelling monks;
the Blessed One said:
"The dwelling place for forest-dwelling monks should be established in an open area."
A certain householder had a monastery built for Upananda; however, he did not reside there himself. Whenever a visiting monk arrived, he would give him lodging, but he took the offerings for himself.
Then a certain monk who was a wearer of the three robes arrived;
he saw that the monastery was empty and asked:
"Whose monastery is this?
The monks replied,
"It belongs to the monk Upananda."
He went there and requested it from him;
he replied: "This is a monastery."
He resided there, thinking, "Whatever profit there is here is mine," and while staying there,
he never once swept that monastery.
The soft cow-dung cake was not given;
meanwhile, he departed from that monastery,
and another monk arrived.
Having also requested [permission] from Upananda, he stayed in that monastery;
he saw that the monastery was filled with refuse,
so he cleared it away, threw out the rubbish, and taking a broom, he stood near a refuse heap.
Then a certain monk saw him and said:
"Venerable one, why do you stand here with a broom held firmly in your hand?"
"Is this broom being set down?
He replied,
"There is someone here standing as a guard over the hand."
"Therefore, he has never even set foot upon a broom.
He replied,
"Such-and-such a person here is a wearer of the three robes (*traicīvarika*)."
"A monk was standing there";
as he was wandering for alms, he saw him and reproached him, and he said:
"Upananda takes the gain; I shall clean his vihāra.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
The Blessed One has said: "He who receives the gains must sweep the monastery;
the dedication of merit (dakṣiṇā) should be proclaimed in the names of the deceased donors."
The elder of the Saṅgha was reciting a verse for the sake of the deceased donors;
a certain householder came to the monastery and heard it.
He assigned the dedication of the gift;
he approached him and said,
"Noble one, if I have a monastery built, will you also dedicate the gift in my name?"
He said, "Build it well; I shall give you instructions.
Thereupon, that householder had a monastery constructed.
In that regard, he had given nothing at all and remained entirely empty;
then, he was seen by that householder.
Having arrived at the monastery, he said: "Venerable sir, my monastery stands empty; no monk resides there."
The senior monk of the Saṃgha said: "Good sir, it must be steamed. That householder replied:
"Noble one, it was built on saline, barren ground;
how can it be heated? "Householder, I did not say that with this intention; rather, I meant that there is no profit there."
He said,
"Noble one, now I shall clothe with a robe whoever resides in my monastery.
Thinking, "Thus a gain is obtained," Upananda gradually took it for himself as if it were his own share.
He continued to dwell in that very place;
it remained empty until a certain alms-collecting monk, who was paying homage at a shrine, arrived at Śrāvastī.
He saw that monastery was empty;
he asked the monks,
"To whom does this monastery belong?"
They replied:
"This monastery belongs to the Saṅgha, but it has been assigned to the monk Upananda";
he then approached Upananda.
"This monastery has been assigned to you; I shall stay here.
He replied, "Do so."
He remained there;
as an alms-collector,
he was skillful and diligent.
Therefore, it is smeared and swept every day;
there are five advantages in sweeping:
one's own mind becomes serene.
The mind of another becomes serene; the deities become joyful;
and one accumulates roots of merit conducive to a pleasing appearance.
"Upon the dissolution of the body, the Sugata will be reborn in a heavenly world among the gods.
Those who see that monastery smeared and swept go and inform the householder;
having heard this, he experiences great joy.
Then, at another time, he came there himself and saw that the monastery was likewise smeared and swept;
he became inspired with faith and covered that alms-collecting monk with a cloth.
Upananda heard this;
he went with great haste and said,
"Alms-collector, this monastery has been assigned to me."
"Give me a cloth," he said.
The alms-collector reflected:
"This man is motivated by gain; if I do not give it to him, he will nevertheless seize it by force and have me expelled from the monastery."
"He handed it over to him";
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
Whomever he favors, for that person alone does he exercise his power of favor;
yet Upānanda’s gain was only for the rainy season—
thus the world, though fond of virtue, tormented itself along with its sons and wives again and again.
Faithful brahmin householders bestow gifts upon those endowed with virtuous qualities;
they invite forest-dwelling monks and provide them with a meal.
However, while the forest-dwelling monks have gone to eat within the houses, the monasteries are plundered by thieves.
The Blessed One said:
"One should depart after locking the door and taking the key";
yet thieves who take what is not given break in using a counter-key.
The Blessed One said: "One should go after having stationed a monk as a guardian;
one must ensure that he has no lack of alms-food."
Those who take what is not given go along taking hold of another monk; he says,
"Release the door!"
The Blessed One said:
"One must make an inquiry as to whether he is with fever or free from fever;
if he says he is with fever, he must not be released."
Then he said, "It should be called 'free from fever';
however, a forest-dwelling monk should provide half-branches.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"A forest-dwelling monk should maintain a 'half-branch' (ardhaśākhā)";
the monks did not know what kind of thing a half-branch was,
so the Blessed One said:
"Monks, a dog should be given half a branch and the remains of his alms-bowl.
Wilderness-dwelling monks kept dogs;
they scratched up the courtyard of the stupa and the monastery with their claws and defiled them with excrement and urine."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk who is a dog-keeper."

A monk who keeps dogs must rise early in the morning and inspect the courtyard of the stūpa and the monastery; whatever has been scratched by their claws should be smoothed over, and excrement and urine should be cleared away.
If a monk who keeps dogs does not undertake and abide by the rules of proper conduct as they have been prescribed, [he commits an offense].
The Venerable Upananda was committing an offense; he was serving as the senior monk of the Saṅgha in a certain monastery.
When a certain elder of the Saṅgha arrived there,
Upananda reflected:
"Having been the elder of the Saṅgha in this monastery, I must now become the second elder."
"I am going to another monastery";
he went to another monastery;
then he departed from that monastery.
Whatever gain belonged to the second elder in that [assembly] became the property of the community elder;
he reflected:
"In this case as well, my own gain is here."
"In that case too, I would have that same gain;
why should I take on the office of senior of the Saṅgha without purpose? Thinking thus, he set out for the monastery with great haste.
Having entered the monastery where the beds and seats were assigned by half, he said:
"Assign the monastery according to seniority."
The monks, thinking that [the time] had passed, did not recite [the scriptures];
Upananda said:
"Venerable ones, why do you let the Teacher's dispensation vanish while he is still present?"
"Assign the monastery according to seniority.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
If someone has gone on business for the sake of the Saṅgha or for a stūpa, his bedding and seating should be assigned according to seniority, except in cases where it follows the order of arrival.

Upānanda, out of excessive greed, entered the rains retreat in two monasteries, thinking, "I shall obtain the gains belonging to both monasteries. When the rains had ended, he sought those gains; however, they were not obtained there.
Nor did he do so toward another;
he reviled the monks who were assigned to the lodgings.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Since he has completed the rains retreat, the gains belonging to him must be given.
The monks then gave [the gains] from both monasteries as well.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, one should not give from both dwellings;
they should give from only one."
Other monks criticized, reviled, and complained, saying:
"Why is [the robe] given from a single source to one who has spent the rains retreat in two different monasteries?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Half and half should be given from both monasteries as well,
but a monk must not enter two monasteries."
If he approaches [a monastery], he incurs an offense of transgression,
provided that a certain householder has had two monasteries built.
One [robe] was for the forest-dwellers, the second for those living near villages;
it was the established practice of that community of monks who had spent the rains retreat at Gṛhapati to clothe each individual monk with a robe.
Taking the cloths, he set out for the forest monastery;
Upananda heard that alms were being distributed at the forest monastery.
He sent word to Nanda, saying,
"If any gain is offered here, you shall take it," and having said this, he set out in haste for the forest monastery;
there he was seen by that householder.
He reflected:
"From the way his footsteps fall,
he has gone to the forest monastery."
"What is appropriate here?
For now, I shall give it right here in this village monastery;
afterwards, I will give it there."
Having turned back, he began to distribute the pieces of cloth;
Nanda extended his hand,
and the householder gave him a piece of cloth.
He stretched it out again;
the householder said: "Noble sir, the cloth has been given to you."
"Why do you stretch it out further? he asked.
He replied, "Householder, Upananda has spent the rains retreat in your monastery; I am requesting what belongs to him."
The householder said:
"Noble sir, giving with one's own hand is praised by the Blessed One;
I shall give with my very own hand."
Ashamed, he remained silent;
Upananda observed:
"This householder is taking a long time."
Thinking, "I shall go to the village-dwelling," he went to the village-dwelling monastery and asked Nanda: "Noble one, was my cloth taken?"
He related the events exactly as they had occurred;
the householder, having gone by another path to the forest monastery and distributed the banners, departed;
Upananda, however, ran back toward the forest monastery.
As many as the cloths were distributed,
he— due to excessive greed for gain from both monasteries— fell away from that profit;
he grieved, was distressed, and lamented.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how Upananda has fallen from his cloth due to excessive greed.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that this man, out of excessive greed, caused his food to be cut off;
listen to how it happened in the past. [This is] the story of the dog who was too greedy (a previous birth of Upananda)."
Long ago, monks, on both banks of a river there were two monasteries:
one for those who receive alms from the community, and the second for those who live on alms-food.
Now, there was a certain dog who was accustomed to the sound of the wooden gong;
having heard the sound of the gong, it would go to the monastery where the monks received their alms-food,
and those monks would give him the remains from their alms-bowls.
Having consumed that, he went to the monastery of the alms-collectors;
there too, having eaten the remains from his bowl, he departed as he pleased.
Then, at another time, a gain of food was obtained for the spontaneously born alms-collectors.
At that very moment, the gong was struck;
hearing the sound of the gong, that "gong-dog" began to cross the river.
When he had reached the middle, the gong was struck again at the monastery where the community was receiving alms.
With his enthusiasm broken, he began to turn back;
carried far away by the current and fallen from both [banks],
what do you think, monks?
He who was that dog Gaṇḍī at that time and on that occasion was none other than this very Upananda;
even then, through excessive greed, he fell away from both [worlds],
and now too, through excessive greed, he has fallen away from both.
Therefore, monks, a monk must not act with excessive greed; if he does so, he commits an offense of transgression. Summary verse: (Śay-v 42)
In Kāśī, there was quarreling, the distribution of provisions for the sick, and the time of night;
[the Buddha ordained] trees, open ground, and grassy plots as the convention for those who distribute [robes].
Precautions to be taken against quarrelsome monks:
The Venerable Upāli questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Suppose, for instance, monks hear that other monks are coming who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, and makers of disputes."
"Those who create disputes and litigations will accuse and remind us, whether out of shamelessness or for the sake of victory. How, then, should those [monks] respond to them?
Upāli, when resident monks hear that monks who create quarrels are approaching, they should prepare three assigners of lodgings.
There are six assigners of lodgings and three allocators of lodgings. Which are they?
Those for the winter, those for the summer, and those for the rainy season.
What are the six recipients of bedding and seating?

Every monastery (*vihāra*) is to be assigned; every vicinity of the monastery (*vihārasāmantaka*); every enclosure (*parigaṇa*); every vicinity of the enclosure (*parigaṇasāmantaka*); every pleasure grove (*ārāma*); and every vicinity of the pleasure grove (*ārāmasāmantaka*).
If someone says, "Assign a monastery," one should say, "This has already been assigned."
"Point out the vicinity of the monastery; this too has been pointed out.
Point out the enclosure; this too has been pointed out. Point out the vicinity of the enclosure; this too has been pointed out."

"Point out the monastery; this too has been pointed out. Point out the vicinity of the monastery; this too has been pointed out. They, being without a dwelling and without a fixed location, will give rise to some fault."
Thereafter, when their impulses have subsided, their adversaries have departed, and their enemies have gone, the bedding and seating should be assigned according to seniority;
so it was said by the Blessed One:
"Bedding and seating should be assigned according to seniority.
[This concerns] the care of sick monks and the mischief of Upananda once more.
Now, there was a certain monk who was ill.
An elder monk arrived; according to seniority, a cell belonging to him was assigned,
yet he was the most junior of all.
He did not enter another dwelling;
he was addressed by that monk:
"Venerable one, this dwelling has been assigned to me."
"Go forth," he said;
he replied, "I am ill; wait until I have recovered."
That monk was cruel;
he was cast out by him and placed in a lotus pond.
Eventually, the brahmins and householders arrived at the monastery.
Desiring to see him, they beheld that monk and said:
"Venerable ones, has this monk passed away?"
"O gentle-faced ones,
he has not passed away; then for what reason was he placed here?"
An elder bhikṣu arrived, and this cell belonging to him was assigned to that elder;
therefore, he was turned out and settled here.
"We are noble householders who, out of consideration, have removed you from the houses of the sick;
you are renunciants,
and your Teacher is compassionate."
"How then do you expel one who is ill?
They reproached, reviled, and censured them.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, an exemption from duties concerning property should be granted to a sick monk. Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"A sick monk must be granted exemption from his duties," [the Buddha said].
To this, the Venerable Upananda replied with a "hum" and remained silent.
Then, thinking, "In six or seven days the bedding and furniture will be assigned," he remained there with a bandage bound around his leg.
The monks assigned to assign lodgings, thinking he was ill, assigned that cell to him;
he remained there with his bandage removed among the assigned lodgings.
Then he was asked by the monks who were visiting the sick: "Has the Elder's foot recovered?"
He said: "The Blessed One has not stated that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
so what [is it] for me? (Śay-v 44)
"Will the illness become permanent? They replied, "Venerable sir, you have recovered quickly."
"Alas, he is ill with the decay of an aeon!
He said:
"Do you wish to cast me into a ruined dwelling?"
The monks of little learning reproached, censured, and spoke in disapproval, saying:
"How is it now that the monks, though not ill, accept the relinquishment of dwellings?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said: "Therefore, monks, the relinquishment of property for one who is ill for the duration of a kalpa must not be given, nor should it be accepted by him."
If one does so, one incurs an offense of transgression. The various blessings for those men who master the Vinaya:
The summary verse for the six pentads:
One's own moral discipline is placed foremost, and it is moreover unattached.
Birth is born of light, and it is indeed an obstacle.
Having placed the offense last, the summary of the alms-food is extracted;
having placed the intermediate summary first, there is another, namely the internal and that of others.
Having been composed for the benefit of many people, this constitutes the first pentad.
The Blessed One established the Sūtras and the Mātṛkās among gods and humans, and the Sūtras among the nāgas.
The Vinaya, however, is profound, appearing profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, full of many intentional nuances (*saṃdhi*), and connected with worldly terminology.
Monks, because of its profundity, its many intentional nuances, and its connection with worldly terminology, do not venture to recite the Vinaya.
And this is the natural law (*dharmatā*): for whichever limb of the teaching is being neglected, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak in high praise of it.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, there are five advantages for a person who is a bearer of the Vinaya. What are the five?"
He is held in high esteem by the fourfold assembly;
his instruction and admonition are not dependent on others;
and he becomes the keeper of the inner treasury of the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, future, and present.
Having reached the pinnacle of other ascetics and brahmins, he stands there;
he is engaged for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, and for the endurance of the true Dharma. This is the intermediate summary verse.
One's own moral conduct, visiting [the teacher], remorse, and being confident—
having performed these together with the Dharma, it becomes the second pentad.
There are five advantages for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are the five?
His own aggregate of ethical discipline becomes well-guarded and well-concealed.
He becomes worthy of being approached by the fourfold assembly;
he becomes a refuge for those persons who are overcome by remorse;
he dwells with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha.
He grasps the adversary within his own true Dharma; the intermediate summary consists of non-attachment, the determination of meaning, and likewise the training precepts.
And there should also be two Ālokas; thus, the third [section] consists of five verses.
There are five further advantages for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are the five?
He extracts the meaning without being entangled.
He becomes well-ascertained regarding the determination of the meaning;
his training precepts are well-grasped;
and he dwells frequently with a mind filled with light.
He brings light to future generations;
the summary verse says: "Light, radiance, and brilliance, with little concern, and by means of the non-empty."
There are five further advantages for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are the five? They are born into the light. (Śay-v 46)
That direction appears to me as illuminated and radiant; I dwell with little concern toward that direction,
and that direction in which a person who upholds the Vinaya resides appears to me as not empty.
The summary verse: Origination, then designation, and indeed further designation;
prohibition and authorization—this is the fifth pentad.
There are five other benefits for a person who upholds the Vinaya; what are the five?
He knows the origin [of an offense].
He understands designation, he understands non-designation,
and he understands rejection.
He recognizes the formal authorization.
*Uddāna:* ... [omitted] ... there are five further advantages in a person who is a holder of the Vinaya.
Which five?
He knows what is an obstacle; he knows what is not an obstacle.
He instructs and exhorts; he is capable of providing the formal support (niśraya) for his co-residents and pupils.
There are five further benefits for a person who maintains the Vinaya;
what are the five?
He knows an offense.
He knows what is not an offense, he knows what is a grave offense, and the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra has been fully expounded to him. (Śay-v 47)

Among them, Upāli was the foremost of those who mastered and knew the Vinaya. Because the Blessed One had spoken in praise of the Vinaya, saying, "The teaching of the Vinaya," the elder monks began to study the Vinaya with great enthusiasm. At that time, the Venerable Upāli was the preeminent among those skilled in the origins and the arising of the Vinaya.
Thinking, "The elder monks are mastering the Vinaya," he began to teach it with great reverence;
consequently, he became pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically exhausted.
Those who know and those who inquire [asked him].
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, ask knowing;
they do not ask unknowing.
They ask at the proper time; they do not ask when the time has passed; they ask what is connected to the goal.
They do not ask questions that are connected with what is unbeneficial;
for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have destroyed the bridge regarding questions connected with what is unbeneficial.
In this regard, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know the proper time for a question that is connected with what is beneficial.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why is the monk Upāli so pale, so wan, emaciated, weak, haggard, and physically exhausted? He replied:

The Blessed One spoke in praise of the Vinaya, and having heard this, the elder monks began to study the Vinaya with great enthusiasm. The venerable Upāli, thinking that the elder monks were receiving the Vinaya with reverence, began to teach it out of respect for them.
Consequently, he became pale, emaciated, weak, haggard, and physically exhausted.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk who gives a formal recitation (uddesa).
A monk who gives a formal recitation must do so by means of the four noble paths."
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
a monk who receives a formal recitation (*uddeśa*) must receive that recitation while maintaining the three noble postures.
If a junior monk comes to receive the recitation from a monk who is giving it while the latter is walking, [the junior monk] should wait until he has stopped.

And having performed the proper etiquette, asked about his physical well-being, and bowed his body with a straightforward mind and reverence, he should receive the recitation by stepping back one step at a time.
Alternatively, if the other is senior, he should ask about his well-being, bow his body, and with a straightforward mind and reverence, receive the recitation by stepping back one step at a time.

If [the teacher] comes while [the student] is standing and the student is junior, he should perform the proper salutation (*sāmīcī*), inquire after his health, squat down (*utkuṭuka*), or sit on a lower seat, and with an upright mind and reverence, receive the recitation (*uddeśa*). If [the student] is senior, he should inquire after his health, remain in a squatting posture, or sit on a lower seat, and with an upright mind and reverence, receive the recitation.
Just as it is for one who is standing, so it should be applied for one who is sitting or lying down:

the monk who gives the recitation should give the recitation having made it well-practiced, thoroughly familiarized, and free from doubt; the monk who receives the recitation should also receive the recitation having asked well, grasped it properly, and made it free from doubt.

If the monk who gives the recitation and the monk who receives the recitation do not undertake and abide by the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed, they commit an offense of transgression.
This was the mischief of the six monks.
The monks of the group-of-six, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at a monastery at night and were assigned lodgings by the monks according to their acquaintances;
they said, "Venerable ones, why do you stand here? Summon the assigner of bedding and seats."
They asked: "For what purpose? [The reply was:
"To assign the lodgings.
They said:
"You shall sleep comfortably on your beds and seats, and when the night has turned to dawn, you will dedicate [the merit]," they said.
But those who were obstructed replied:
"While you remain standing, you are causing the Teacher's dispensation to disappear!"
If there is remorse, point out the bedding and seating according to seniority;
you are strong in speech.
The assigner of lodgings, being terrified, made the assignment;
the group of six monks took their lodgings at the end of the row and lay down; by the time the junior monks were being assigned their places, the night had turned to dawn.
The group of six monks, rising very quickly, said:
"Venerable ones, take up your bedding and seats;
let us go."
They were addressed by the monks:
"Venerable ones, for the sake of a single night you have troubled the entire community of monks throughout the whole night; oh, would that you would stay right here!
They replied:
"Nanda and Upananda, let us go to Śrāvastī together with the Savātala monks. Having said this, they departed.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
On the occasion of this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
Therefore, monks, lodgings should not be assigned at night;
if they arrive at night, they should be accommodated according to their acquaintance with one another.

A monk from a certain country, who had come to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the caitya, was unskilled regarding the proper alms-round there. Rising very early in the morning, he approached the Blessed One, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, and [paid respects] to the elder monks; then he entered Śrāvastī for alms.
As he was wandering for alms, the time arrived; leaning against the base of a wall right there, he began to perform his meal.
And Anāthapiṇḍada set out along that same path, intending to pay homage to the shrine.
He saw him and said,
"Noble one, having gone forth in this teaching which is so universally pleasing, why do you act as a troublemaker?
He replied:
"Venerable one, what is this clamor?
Do you not see that the time is near?
He replied:
"Why have you not come to my house?
"What is your name?
"Anāthapiṇḍada."
"I have heard in various sūtras that there is a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada, Anāthapiṇḍada; yet I do not know you, nor do I know your home."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada reflected:
"This monk has come from afar and does not know the local customs;
surely he does not know me, nor my house."

"What would be appropriate here at this time? I shall have a walkway constructed from Śrāvastī as far as the Jeta Grove. Having understood this, he approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, visiting monks who are unskilled in the proper range for alms-gathering, while wandering for alms, will pass the time and perform their meal-eating by leaning against the base of a wall.
Lacking faith, they will disparage the noble ones on this account.
Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would have a walkway constructed between Śrāvastī and the Jetavana."
"Whoever's turn it shall be at which time, he shall partake of almsfood there.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, householder, I authorize you; have it made."
Therefore, he had walkways constructed between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove;
whichever monk’s turn it was, he would perform his meal duties there.
Other monks suffered from a lack of drinking water;
therefore, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had a well constructed there and a cartload of the three pungent substances and the three myrobalans was brought up.
That water became delicious and excellent, becoming renowned throughout the entire world.
The multitude of people, having heard [of this], arrived;
the monks, residents of Śrāvastī, restrained them.
"We are noble ones who attend to you with all necessary provisions,
yet you withhold water that is common to all the world.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"They should not be prevented";
thus, women asked the monks for drinking water.
The monks did not grant it;
the Blessed One said:
"It must be granted. Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"The female sex is a universal snare, a bond of Māra.
Monks, while offering water, became lustful toward women;
eventually, a certain woman endowed with beauty and youth felt an excessive longing for a young monk.
He asks for that water;
even one who has regard for her and a mind of attachment,
though being restrained, gives it with an uninterrupted stream, and she likewise gazes upon him.
"She drank water that had turned poisonous; she has passed away. Monks who were not seeking profit reproached, reviled, and censured him.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin story, the Blessed One said:
"If a woman is full of longing toward a monk and her mind is bound to him, one must not give [the robe] to her oneself."
Furthermore, one must not give water to a woman in an unbroken stream;
rather, the stream of water should be interrupted at intervals, or one should say, "Fill your cupped hands and drink," otherwise one commits an offense of transgression.
At that time, those who were offering the first alms-food in Jeta’s Grove began to give it right there;
the group-of-six monks heard of this, went to the walking-path, and stood there.
They ask for that by which the non-sticky alms-food is brought; if it is milk-rice, they hold out a bowl;
if it is a drink or gruel, [they do likewise].
They say:
"The Saṃgha possesses great supernormal power; that Saṃgha is of great majesty."
"Give it to the Saṃgha";
in this way, [the distribution of] solid foods and so forth should be arranged.
The monks, having little need [for such things], reproach, revile, and speak against [this].
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said: "A monk must not appropriate another's gain."
If he assembles [the community], he incurs an offense of transgression;
for it was said by the Blessed One:
"A monk must not participate in the gains belonging to others.
Thus, monks might go to another monastery for some business;
when they have arrived there, the time [for the distribution] draws near.
Out of remorse, they did not eat;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and on this occasion the Blessed One said:

"One should not go there intentionally; otherwise, if the time for eating has already passed for those who have gone, one should eat, and no remorse should be felt here, for this is a time of hardship.
(Śay-v 52) Thus, a period of scarcity prevails.
The monks went to another monastery;
seeing the monks there eating, they desired to eat as well,
but out of remorse they did not partake.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"If that which was not taken in the previous monastery is being distributed in unlimited quantity, it should be taken."
Now, if the authority of the monks has been established, it must not be accepted; if one accepts it, one commits an offense of transgression.
(The nefarious deeds of the monks Aśvaka and Punarvasuka.)
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country of Kāśī, arrived at Kiṭāgiri.
At that time, two monks named Aśvaka and Punarvasuka were residing at Kiṭāgiri; they heard:
"The Blessed One, having wandered on tour through the Kāśī countries, will come here together with the community of monks.
Having heard this, they reflected again:
"The monks will, in the presence of the Teacher, reproach us or remind us, whether out of shamelessness or out of a desire for retaliation."
What if we were to establish a large monastery for the sake of the Blessed One and appoint three assigners of lodgings and six receivers of lodgings concerning the monks?
Who are the three assigners of lodgings?
The winter [settlement], the summer [settlement], and the rainy season [settlement];
what are the six types of recipients of bedding and seats?
The entire monastery is to be assigned,
the entire vicinity of the monastery, and the entire enclosure.
The entire vicinity of the monastery enclosure, the entire grove, and the entire vicinity of the grove—
if they say, "Appoint a dwelling for us," one should say, "This has already been appointed."

"Point out a surrounding area for the monastery; this one has been pointed out. Point out the vicinity of the monastery; this too has been pointed out. Point out a grove; this too has been pointed out."
"Appoint the vicinity of the monastery; this too is appointed.
They were without a dwelling and without a fixed residence, thinking, "They will not reproach us or remind us, whether out of shamelessness or because they are indifferent.
Those two had three assigners of lodgings appointed.
There were six who took charge of the lodgings;
meanwhile, the Blessed One arrived at Kiṭāgiri,
and those two had already prepared a monastery for the Blessed One.
The monks said:
"Venerable ones, designate the lodgings and the monastery.
They replied:
The monastery has been assigned as previously indicated;
the courtyard has been assigned;
that too has been assigned.
"Designate the vicinity of the monastery"; that too was designated;
"Designate the vicinity of the enclosure."
That too was assigned;
assign a monastery grove;
that too was assigned.
"Designate the vicinity of the monastery";
that too was designated.
Since they did not designate it in its entirety, a loud noise and a great clamor arose at the edge of the monastery.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, being knowers, ask as knowers; not being ignorant, they do not ask;
they ask at the proper time.
They do not ask what is past its time;
they ask what is connected with the goal, and they do not ask what is disconnected from the goal.
The suspension of the bridge is for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, when a question is associated with what is meaningless;
in that regard, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know the proper time for a question associated with what is meaningful. Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned the Venerable Ānanda.
"Ānanda, why has this loud noise, this great clamor, and the roar of a great multitude arisen at the edge of the monastery?
He replied: "The two monks Aśvaka and Punarvasuka have made three assignments for lodgings and furniture with reference to the monks."
There were six who took charge of the lodgings;
the monks did not obtain lodgings,
and because of that, this loud noise, great clamor, and roar of a great crowd arose at the edge of the monastery.

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, it was with reference to monks who cause strife that I established three assigners of lodgings and six receivers of lodgings, but not for those who abide in their natural state."

Therefore, monks should not appoint three assigners of lodgings and six receivers of lodgings with reference to monks who are in their natural state. If they do so, they commit an offense of transgression.
(The mischief of the Six Monks again.)
While the Blessed One was wandering on tour through the Kośala country, he arrived for the night’s stay at a certain forest hermitage in a small village together with the community of monks.
The group of six monks, having set aside one beautiful tree for the sake of the Blessed One,
took other beautiful trees for themselves.
Hollow trees were found by the elder and senior monks;
King Prasenajit of Kośala heard of this and went out to meet them with a fourfold army.
Having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, he searched for the elder monks;
eventually, he saw the group-of-six monks stationed beneath beautiful trees,
while the elder monks were under hollow trees.
Having uttered "Hum," he approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
King Prasenajit of Kosala, seated to one side, [said:]
He said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I am a consecrated Kṣatriya king, the master of all jewels produced within my realm;
every exquisite object belongs to me."
Whatever remained was distributed as appropriate among the queens, the princes, the ministers, and the army commanders; the Blessed One, the Supreme Dharma King,
as well as the great śrāvakas such as the noble Kauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and Revata, stayed in hollow trees.
But the group of six [monks] [sat] under beautiful trees,
thinking, "Oh, would that the Blessed One, out of compassion, were to arrange even the trees according to seniority!
The Blessed One consented to King Prasenajit of Kośala by remaining silent.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, understanding through his silence that the Blessed One had accepted [the invitation], bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed.
Regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, even trees, as well as sacrificial altars and grassy plots, should be assigned according to seniority."
The Blessed One said: "Even trees should be assigned according to seniority, as well as open spaces and grassy plots.
However, the monks were assigning them themselves.
The Blessed One said:
"A monk who assigns dwellings should be appointed.
The monks appointed [monks] without distinction.
The Blessed One said:
"Endowed with five qualities, a monk appointed as the assigner of lodgings (vihāroddeśaka) who has not been appointed should not be appointed, and one who has been appointed should be dismissed."
By which five?
He acts out of desire, he acts out of hatred, he acts out of delusion, he acts out of fear, and he does not know the difference between an assigned and an unassigned dwelling.
One who possesses these five qualities, though appointed as a distributor of dwellings, is not to be appointed [if not already so], and one who is already so appointed is to be removed.
And one who has been appointed should be dismissed;
however, one endowed with five qualities who is not yet appointed as the assigner of dwellings should be appointed, and once appointed, he should not be dismissed.
By which five?
He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion, and he knows what has been assigned and what has not been assigned.
Endowed with these five qualities, one who assigns dwellings, even if not yet appointed, should be appointed.
And once he has been approved, he must not be set aside; furthermore, he is to be approved in this manner:

having prepared the seating and struck the ghaṇṭā, and having questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha is seated and assembled, [the candidate] is to be encouraged as previously described, up until the point of being exhorted.
"Are you, so-and-so by name, able to designate the dwellings for the Saṃgha?
If he is able, he should say, "I am able.
Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*).
May the venerable Saṃgha listen:
this monk named so-and-so, the assigner of dwellings, is able to assign dwellings for the Saṃgha; if it seems the right time to the Saṃgha and if it should approve, [let it authorize him].
"Let the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha should appoint such-and-such a person as the assigner of dwellings; this is the motion (jñapti).
The formal act (karman) is to be performed:
Let the venerable Saṃgha listen."

This monk named so-and-so, the assigner of dwellings, is capable of assigning dwellings for the Saṃgha. Therefore, the Saṃgha appoints this monk named so-and-so as the assigner of dwellings. Those venerable ones who approve of appointing this monk named so-and-so as the assigner of dwellings should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak. The Saṃgha has appointed this monk named so-and-so as the assigner of dwellings.
The Saṃgha has consented and authorized this, since it is silent;
thus do I hold it.

Just as with the assigner of dwellings, so it is with the assigner of meals, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of solid foods, the distributor of miscellaneous items, the keeper of utensils, the keeper of robes, the distributor of robes, and the keeper of rain-cloaks.
The distributor of the rainy-season robes is the one who sends [messages].
A monk serving as the superintendent of the monastery who possesses five qualities, even if not yet appointed, should not be appointed.
And he should be granted leave;
by which five [factors]?
He acts out of desire, he acts out of hatred, he acts out of delusion, or he acts out of fear.

He does not know what is pleasing and what is displeasing; however, a monk endowed with five qualities who has been appointed as the superintendent of the monastery (prāsādavārika) should be appointed if he has not yet been so appointed, and if he has been so appointed, he should not be dismissed.
By which five?
He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear; and he discerns what is graceful and what is ungraceful.
The summary verse:
The assigner of dwellings and meals, the distributor of rice-gruel and solid food,
the guardian of whatever goods there may be, and the two types of robes.
The rain-cloak, the cowherd, the distributor, the messenger, and likewise the superintendent of the monastery—
these are remembered as the twelve individuals.
The Section on Bedding and Seating is completed.
